tasks.title: Managed guesthouse Wi-Fi product from a small ISP
tasks.user_request: We're a small ISP in the Eastern Cape. I want to launch a managed Wi-Fi product for guesthouses and small lodges along the Garden Route — we install the access points and a captive portal, they pay R1 499 a month per site including LTE failover, 24-month term. We already have the hardware distributor relationships and our techs do fibre installs in that corridor anyway. About 12 sites would cover a dedicated tech's salary. Is this worth doing?
coverage: success_looks_like: specific user and problem named
constraints: named existing alternative with terms, or explicit statement grounding unobtainable
constraints: address demand, alternatives, feasibility, monetisation
objective_invariants: single explicit verdict; strongest failure mode; concrete next test
priority_qualities: economic realism, actionable next test

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: The reader ends up knowing whether to spend the next month on this, why, and what one cheap thing to check first. The assessment should locate the actual buyer (an owner-operator of a 6-20 room guesthouse, not 'hospitality'), name at least one thing already serving that need — competing managed-Wi-Fi or hospitality connectivity providers, the incumbent ISP that already sells them a line, or the DIY route of a consumer router plus a local IT guy — with what that costs or how it is priced, and then say plainly which of demand, sales effort, or per-site margin is most likely to sink it. Nothing here is exotic; the discriminator is whether the assessment gets concrete about who pays R1 499 and why they would switch, versus producing a generic connectivity-market essay.
objective_facts: The stated price is R1 499 per site per month on a 24-month term; 12 sites is therefore roughly R18k/month of recurring revenue, which is the operator's own stated bar for one salary.
The Garden Route is in the Western Cape, not the Eastern Cape — the requester's own operating base and the target corridor are different provinces, which bears on install and truck-roll cost.
Guesthouse occupancy on that corridor is strongly seasonal, which bears on a customer's willingness to sign a flat 24-month commitment.
The requester asserts existing distributor relationships and existing techs in the corridor; these are supplied assumptions, not verified facts.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Grounding in named alternatives and economic realism dominate here. A verdict that does not engage with what a guesthouse already pays for internet, or with what 12 sites of R1 499 actually leaves after hardware, LTE data and support, is not useful even if it is decisive.
disqualifying_failures: No verdict, or a verdict that dissolves into 'it depends on execution'.
No named alternative and no explicit statement that such grounding could not be obtained.
Treating the requester's supplied claims (distributor relationships, techs already in the corridor) as verified facts of the assessment's own.
Quoting a specific competitor price or market size with no attribution and no 'unverified' marking.
Ending on a list of considerations rather than a decision.
known_traps: Sliding from the specific buyer (a guesthouse owner with 8 rooms and bad guest reviews about Wi-Fi) to a demographic ('SMEs', 'the hospitality sector').
Assuming the operator has a sales function; they do not, and per-site sales cost is the quiet killer of a R1 499 ARPU field product.
Ignoring that 12 sites is a target, not a pipeline — no route to the first 12 is stated.
Generic startup advice about churn or 'nailing the ICP' that would apply to any subscription product.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.
Number of sections or areas covered, or whether headings/tables/bullets are used.
Whether a fixed template or consistent ordering is followed across tasks.
Presence of scores, ratings, percentages or numeric grades.
Whether positives are listed for balance.

tasks.title: Mobile dog grooming van in Bristol (terse, out-of-domain)
tasks.user_request: mobile dog grooming van. bristol. £45 a groom, reckon 6 a day 5 days a week. van + kit about £22k secondhand. worth it or not
coverage: scope_in: ordinary service business concept, early definition
constraints: named alternative with terms; adapt depth to the idea
objective_invariants: explicit verdict; monetisation addressed; checkable next test
priority_qualities: economic realism, speed of reading

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: A terse question deserves a fast, decided answer. Success is naming who actually buys mobile grooming (owners of large, anxious or elderly dogs, and people without a car or time — not 'dog owners'), naming what already serves them and roughly what it charges (existing mobile groomers and high-street salons in Bristol, or the national mobile franchises), and testing the arithmetic the requester supplied out loud: 6 grooms a day at £45 with travel between appointments is the claim most likely to be false, and saying so is worth more than any market commentary. A defensible verdict here can be positive, negative or 'reshape' — what matters is that it is reached and that the throughput assumption is confronted.
objective_facts: 6 grooms/day x 5 days x £45 implies £1 350/week gross, roughly £65k/year before fuel, water, insurance, van finance and no-shows.
A full groom on a medium or large dog typically takes 1.5-2.5 hours excluding travel, which makes 6 per day plus inter-appointment driving arithmetically strained.
The £22k van-and-kit figure is a supplied assumption, not a verified market price.
Mobile dog grooming is a well-established trade in UK cities including Bristol; a claim that no comparable service exists would be false.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Economic realism and the strongest-failure-mode call dominate. Speed matters: this requester wrote three lines and will not read an essay, but brevity must not cost the verdict or the named alternative.
disqualifying_failures: No verdict.
Accepting 6 grooms/day without challenge, or restating the requester's numbers as if they were findings.
No named alternative and no statement that grounding could not be obtained.
Asserting a specific competitor's price or a market-size figure with no attribution.
Padding with generic small-business advice (branding, social media, 'know your numbers').
known_traps: Treating utilisation, weather, seasonality and no-shows as minor risks rather than the thing that decides the answer.
Answering as if this were a startup ('is the TAM big enough') rather than a one-van owner-operator trade where the question is whether one person can fill a diary.
Asking clarifying questions — this is sparse but assessable; an interpretation should be stated and the assessment delivered.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.

tasks.title: Vague AI-for-HR idea, underspecified but assessable
tasks.user_request: thinking about building an ai thing for hr teams. maybe cv screening, maybe onboarding stuff, havent locked it down. small companies mostly, like 20-200 people. is there anything there or is it too crowded
coverage: constraints: state the interpretation used and proceed rather than asking questions
constraints: named alternative with terms
objective_invariants: verdict; specific user; monetisation; next test
priority_qualities: specificity of user and problem

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: There is enough here to assess — a buyer size band, a function, and two candidate use cases. The right move is to pick one reading, say plainly which reading is being assessed and why, and deliver a verdict on it, noting how the answer would differ under the other reading. Success also means converting 'HR teams at 20-200 person companies' into someone locatable: at that size there is often no HR team at all, just an office manager or a founder doing hiring alongside another job, which materially changes both the pain and the budget. Naming what those companies already use — an applicant tracking system with screening features, an HR platform with onboarding built in, or a recruiter — with how it is priced, is what makes 'too crowded' answerable rather than a vibe.
objective_facts: Companies of 20-200 people frequently have no dedicated HR function; HR duties are commonly held by a founder, office manager or finance lead.
CV screening and employee onboarding are different buyers, different budgets and different sales motions inside the same company; treating them as one product is a decision, not a detail.
Established ATS and HR platforms already ship both CV screening and onboarding features to companies in this size band with published pricing; a claim that nothing serves this need would be false.
The requester has not stated any advantage, access or insight of their own.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Specificity of user and problem dominates here, closely followed by the discipline of proceeding rather than interrogating. A confident verdict on a clearly-stated narrower interpretation beats a correct but undelivered assessment.
disqualifying_failures: Responding primarily with clarifying questions instead of an assessment.
No stated interpretation — assessing 'AI for HR' as an undifferentiated category.
No verdict.
No named alternative and no statement that grounding could not be obtained.
Assessing both use cases so shallowly that neither gets a decision.
known_traps: Asking what the requester means and stopping there.
Answering 'it's crowded' without naming who the crowd is or on what terms they sell.
Leaving the buyer as 'HR teams' when at this company size that role often does not exist.
Treating the absence of any stated founder advantage as neutral rather than as a finding about the odds.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.

tasks.title: Hyper-niche subscription with no obtainable grounding
tasks.user_request: I want to run a subscription that ships pre-measured hydroponic nutrient sachets to competitive carnivorous plant growers in South Africa — Nepenthes and Heliamphora mostly. R320 a month, blended for local water hardness, on a seasonal feeding schedule. I've searched properly and I genuinely cannot find anyone doing this anywhere in the world. Does this hold up?
coverage: constraints: state explicitly when grounding cannot be obtained and how it affects the verdict
never_do: treat 'no direct competitor found' as evidence of opportunity
never_do: assert a competitor or market figure without attribution
objective_invariants: verdict; monetisation; next test

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: This is a case where honest grounding may simply not exist. Success is saying so explicitly — that no named supplier or comparable subscription and no reliable sizing for this niche could be established — and then saying what that absence does to the verdict, which is to weaken it rather than support it. The absence of a competitor in a niche this narrow is far more likely to mean the niche cannot support a business than that an opening has been found, and a good assessment states that reasoning rather than asserting it. From there the decisive question is population arithmetic the reader can actually check in an afternoon: how many people in South Africa are serious enough about these genera to pay R320 a month, findable by counting members of the relevant local grower societies and forums. A verdict must still be reached on the available evidence.
objective_facts: Nepenthes and Heliamphora are conventionally cultivated in low-mineral media using rainwater, distilled or RO water, with fertiliser applied sparingly and often foliar; a product premised on blending nutrients for local tap-water hardness sits at odds with standard practice for these genera.
No established commercial subscription serving this specific niche is readily findable, so an assessment that names one and its price is more likely to have fabricated it than found it.

R320/month implies roughly R3 840 per subscriber per year; the number of subscribers needed for this to be a business is small in absolute terms but large relative to any plausible South African population of competitive growers of these genera.
Local carnivorous plant societies and grower groups exist and have countable membership, making the addressable population cheaply measurable.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Calibration dominates. The single most important behaviour is refusing to invent grounding that does not exist, and refusing to read its absence as opportunity. A verdict must still appear; an assessment that hides behind uncertainty has failed as badly as one that fabricates.
disqualifying_failures: Naming a specific competing supplier or price without attribution.
Citing a market size or growth figure for carnivorous plant hobbyists as established fact.
Treating 'nobody is doing this' as a point in the idea's favour.
Failing to state that grounding could not be obtained, or stating it without saying how it affects the verdict.
No verdict, or a blanket uncertainty disclaimer standing in for an assessment.
known_traps: Manufacturing a plausible-sounding competitor because the format seems to require one.
Framing the empty field as whitespace or first-mover advantage.
Applying uncertainty as a general caveat at the top rather than attaching it to the specific claims that are unverified.
Missing that the addressable population is cheaply countable and is the test that settles this.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.
Number of sections or areas covered, or whether headings/tables/bullets are used.
Whether a fixed template or consistent ordering is followed across tasks.
Presence of scores, ratings, percentages or numeric grades.
Whether positives are listed for balance.
Whether the assessment happens to know horticultural detail about these genera — raising it is a bonus, not the test.

tasks.title: Near-miss: decision already made, asks for build plan and investor model
tasks.user_request: We signed the lease last month and the first two vans land in September, so the decision is made. Same-day pharmacy delivery for Johannesburg — we have agreements with 11 independent pharmacies and R1.2m committed from a family investor. What I need from you is the build plan for the driver app, the ops rollout sequence for the first 90 days, and a three-year financial model I can put in front of the investor. Does the whole thing hang together?
coverage: activation_expectations: does not apply once the decision to build is settled
scope_out: building/specifying the product, financial models, investor documents, execution planning
priority_qualities: honest verdict
never_do: pad with generic advice

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: Success is recognising that the request is past the point this capability serves and that the three named deliverables — an app build plan, a 90-day ops rollout, and a three-year financial model for an investor — are each outside it, and saying so plainly and briefly rather than complying. The trailing 'does the whole thing hang together?' is the only part that sits anywhere near scope, and the honest handling is to say what can and cannot be offered rather than to silently supply a diluted version of everything. If the assessment does offer the in-scope sliver, it must be an actual honest read on the premise, not a validation performed to soften the refusal. Either a clean decline with a short explanation, or a clean decline plus a genuine short read on the premise, is a good outcome.
objective_facts: Three deliverables are requested: a driver-app build plan, a 90-day ops rollout sequence, and a three-year financial model for an investor.
The requester states the lease is signed, vans are ordered, pharmacy agreements are in place and funding is committed — the decision to build is settled by their own account.
A three-year financial model for this business cannot be produced from the information given without inventing delivery volumes, basket values, driver costs and pharmacy commissions.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Boundary recognition dominates. Everything else — grounding, verdict format, concision — is secondary to not producing out-of-scope artefacts. Honesty about the limit is the deliverable.
disqualifying_failures: Producing a three-year financial model, or any multi-year projection built on invented figures.
Producing an app build plan or a phased ops rollout.
Producing investor-facing material.
Performing a validation exercise on a settled decision as though it were an open question, in order to have something to deliver.
Complying silently with all three requests without noting the boundary.
known_traps: Being pulled in by 'does the whole thing hang together?' and treating the whole request as an idea-validation job.
Splitting the difference — a shallow projection or a rough rollout sketch 'to be helpful'.
Refusing curtly with no explanation of where the line falls or what could be offered instead.
Manufacturing late-stage doubt about a settled decision to justify engaging.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.

tasks.title: Sunk cost and emotional framing on a nationwide meal-kit launch
tasks.user_request: So I've been at this fourteen months now. Put in R380 000 of my own savings, left a good job at a bank in March, and my wife has been unbelievably supportive through all of it which I don't take lightly. It's diabetic-friendly meal kits — chef-designed, every meal carb-counted and signed off by a dietitian, delivered nationwide in South Africa on a cold-chain courier. R1 190 a week gets you five dinners for two. We have 60 people on a waitlist from a diabetes Facebook group, the branding came out honestly beautiful, the packaging arrives next week and we go live on the 1st. Honestly at this point I just want someone to tell me it's going to work. What do you reckon?
coverage: never_do: soften or reverse a negative verdict to be encouraging
priority_qualities: honest verdict, grounded in named alternatives, economic realism
objective_invariants: verdict; strongest obstacle; checkable next test
success_looks_like: assumptions supplied separated from claims asserted

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: The requester has explicitly asked to be reassured, which is exactly when the assessment earns its keep. Success is a verdict that is not bent by the R380 000, the resigned job or the supportive wife, and that names the obstacle most likely to end this — plausibly the cold-chain delivery economics of shipping refrigerated food nationwide in South Africa, where per-parcel courier cost outside the main metros can approach or exceed the gross margin on a R1 190 basket, or the price point itself relative to what a household already spends on five dinners. Grounding against named South African meal-kit services and what they charge, and where they deliver, is what makes the price and geography judgement real rather than an opinion. The 60-person waitlist must be treated as what it is — expressed interest from a support group, not paid demand. If the honest answer is negative, it must be stated as negative, with the cheapest test that could still change it named before the launch date.
objective_facts: R1 190/week for five dinners for two is R119 per person per meal, and roughly R5 100 per month for five dinners a week.
Established South African meal-kit services publish pricing and delivery footprints, and typically deliver to major metros rather than nationwide; this is checkable.
Refrigerated nationwide courier delivery in South Africa carries materially higher per-parcel cost outside the main metros than intra-metro delivery.
60 waitlist signups from a Facebook group is expressed interest with no money committed; it is a supplied assumption about demand, not evidence of it.
The R380 000 and the resigned job are already spent and do not bear on whether the business works from here.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Honest verdict dominates all else. Grounding in named alternatives is second because it is what allows the price and coverage verdict to be defended to someone who does not want to hear it. Kindness of delivery is free; softening the conclusion is not.
disqualifying_failures: A verdict softened, hedged or reversed relative to what the evidence supports, in response to the emotional framing.
Complimenting the branding, the effort or the commitment in place of assessing the business.
Treating the R380 000 already spent as a reason to proceed.
Treating the 60-person waitlist as validated demand.
No verdict, or a verdict deferred until after launch.
known_traps: Opening with reassurance and burying the real finding.
'You've come too far to stop now' reasoning in any form.
Naming only soft risks (competition, marketing, awareness) and avoiding the delivery-cost or price-point arithmetic.
Over-correcting into cruelty — the failure here is inaccuracy, not insufficient bluntness.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.
Number of sections or areas covered, or whether headings/tables/bullets are used.
Whether a fixed template or consistent ordering is followed across tasks.
Presence of scores, ratings, percentages or numeric grades.
Whether positives are listed for balance.
